cards.front: What does the WHO mean by rational use of medicines?
cards.back: Patients receive medicines suited to their clinical needs, in doses that match their own requirements, for an adequate period, and at the lowest cost to them and their community. It covers the whole supply-use chain, though prescribing is the clinical core.

cards.front: Which criteria show that a prescription is appropriate?
cards.back: A sound indication; a drug that suits the patient for efficacy, tolerability, safety and cost; a dose, route and duration fitted to the patient; no contraindication, the drug acceptable to the patient, and expected benefit greater than likely harm; correct dispensing with instructions; and follow-up of adherence, benefit and adverse effects.

cards.front: Why should a drug be prescribed by its generic (non-proprietary) name, and when is a brand name better?
cards.back: A generic name is uniform, shorter and easier to remember than many brand names, and it lets the pharmacist supply any manufacturer's product, which is usually cheaper because no brand promotion is paid for. A brand name is safer when product consistency in quality and bioavailability matters and official quality control is weak.

cards.front: Classify: the three names of a drug
cards.text: A {{chemical}} name describes the molecule and is too cumbersome for prescribing; a {{non-proprietary}} name is the accepted generic name, and the WHO recommends {{rINN}} names for new drugs; a {{brand}} name is the manufacturer's trademark and can differ between countries.

cards.front: Why does teaching the prescriber more pharmacology not by itself make prescribing rational?
cards.back: Knowledge is the main determinant of prescribing, but it has been shown repeatedly that improving it alone fails to promote rational use. Other pressures act too: copying teachers and popular doctors, heavy patient load giving routine symptom-based prescribing, imprecise diagnosis, drug promotion and inducements, and patients who expect a pill for every ill.

cards.front: What does the expiry date on a medicine mean, and how long may a manufacturer set it?
cards.back: It is a legal requirement that every product carries its manufacture and expiry dates. The period between them is the life period; the manufacturer guarantees quality under stated storage only up to that date. Under Schedule P (Rule 96, Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940) life periods are mostly 1 to 5 years; other expiry dates may not exceed 5 years unless the licensing authority accepts stability proof.

cards.front: Which antibiotic formulation past its expiry caused renal toxicity in man, and what did it cause?
cards.back: Outdated tetracycline capsules. Their degradation product damaged renal tubules, producing a Fanconi-like picture in the early 1960s. The capsules have since been reformulated to limit degradation.

cards.front: Short note: Irrational prescribing

points: Prescriber habits, copied from teachers or popular doctors
Heavy patient load leading to routine symptom-based prescribing
Imprecise diagnosis, so several drugs are given to cover every possibility
Industry promotion, unrealistic claims and inducements
Patient demand for a 'pill for every ill'; knowledge alone does not fix this
Drug given when none is needed (antibiotic for viral fever or non-specific diarrhoea); compulsive vitamins and tonics
Drug unrelated to the diagnosis (PPI for any abdominal symptom); wrong drug (tetracycline for pharyngitis)
Doubtful-efficacy drugs; wrong route (injection when oral would do); wrong dose or duration (stopping TB treatment early; prolonged post-operative antibiotics)
Unnecessary combinations, costly new drugs where cheaper ones work, unsafe use (corticosteroid for fever), polypharmacy with interaction risk
Delayed relief or cure; more adverse effects; longer hospital stay, more morbidity and mortality
Emergence of microbial resistance
Financial loss to patient and community; loss of trust in the doctor; lower community health standards
Follow the stepwise process of rational prescribing, including monitoring
Use the essential medicines list for procurement and supply, which improves availability, saves cost and promotes rational use
Knowledge alone has not been enough to change prescribing; the other influences above must also be addressed

cards.front: Classify: examples of irrational prescribing
cards.text: Antibiotic for a viral fever is {{use when no drug is needed}}; tetracycline for pharyngitis is {{wrong drug selection}}; corticosteroid for fever is {{unsafe use}}; ciprofloxacin plus tinidazole for any diarrhoea is {{unnecessary combination}}; an injection where tablets would do is {{incorrect route}}.

cards.front: A mother insists on an antibiotic for her child's viral fever. Which irrationality is this, which pressures cause it, and what are the consequences?
cards.back: It is use of a drug when none is needed. Patient demand ('pill for every ill'), the prescriber's wish to give prompt symptomatic relief and imprecise diagnosis all push towards it. Consequences of irrational prescribing include delayed or lost relief, more adverse effects, longer hospital stay, morbidity and mortality, and microbial resistance.

cards.front: An expired tablet is still in the cabinet. Why is it not automatically dangerous, and what would speed the loss of potency?
cards.back: Expiry means quality is no longer assured and the maker is not liable; it does not show the drug has become toxic or lost potency. Most solid oral forms kept unopened stay active for years. High humidity and temperature accelerate degradation, and liquids and injections are less stable (suspensions clump, injections precipitate or discolour). Use beyond the expiry date is still not legally allowed.

cards.front: Essay: Rational use of medicines

points: WHO: right medicine for the clinical need, at an individual dose, for adequate time, at the lowest cost to patient and community
Covers every step of the supply-use chain: selection, procurement, storage, prescribing, dispensing, monitoring, feedback
Appropriate indication, drug, dose-route-duration, patient (no contraindication, benefit above harm)
Correct dispensing with information; monitoring of adherence and effects
Drug when none needed, unrelated to diagnosis, wrong drug, doubtful efficacy, wrong route, dose or duration, unnecessary combinations
Examples: antibiotic for viral fever, PPI for any abdominal symptom, vitamins and tonics
Knowledge alone does not decide: role models, patient load, imprecise diagnosis, promotion and inducements, patient demand
Delayed or lost relief, more adverse effects, longer stay, morbidity and mortality, resistance
Stepwise rational prescribing, patient information, essential medicines lists, P-drug approach, generic names

cards.front: What are the steps of rational prescribing?
cards.back: 1) Establish at least a provisional diagnosis. 2) Define the therapeutic problem and goals (symptom relief, cure, prevention of complications). 3) Select the drug class for each goal. 4) Choose the drug on efficacy, safety, suitability for this patient and cost. 5) Decide route, dose and duration for this patient. 6) Give information and instructions. 7) Monitor adherence, goal achievement and adverse effects, and change therapy as needed.

cards.front: What information must a patient receive when a drug is prescribed?
cards.back: What effect to expect and when; whether the disease is cured or only controlled; what happens if doses are missed; common side effects, told without alarming the patient; how and how long to take it, and which tests are needed; precautions such as not driving after sedating antihistamines or not drinking alcohol with metronidazole. The patient should repeat the instructions back to confirm understanding.

cards.front: Why is rational prescribing more than choosing the correct drug for the diagnosis?
cards.back: It also covers the whole therapeutic set-up: dose, route and duration fitted to the patient, correct dispensing and instructions, and follow-up of adherence, benefit and adverse effects. Therapy is reviewed and changed until the goals are reached, so the job continues after the prescription is handed over.

cards.front: Complete: safe writing of doses
cards.text: Write a {{zero}} before a decimal point (0.1, not .1); never add a {{trailing}} zero (1 mg, not 1.0 mg, which can be read as 10); write {{units}} in full instead of U; and write {{microgram}} in full because the shortened form can be misread as mg.

cards.front: Why do patients become noncompliant, and how can compliance be improved?
cards.back: Noncompliance is a main cause of treatment failure. It is encouraged by symptomless disease, painful chronic conditions, frequent dosing, living alone, hard-to-open packs, lack of transport and personal or cultural beliefs. Compliance improves with good communication with the patient, attention to social and economic conditions, linking doses to a daily routine such as meals, dose organisers, alarms, refill reminders and active patient participation.

cards.front: Short note: Prescription writing

points: Name, professional degree, address and telephone number, so the pharmacist can verify and contact
Signature and licence or registration number
Date written (and time for hospital orders)
Patient's full name and address; age or date of birth and sex are often added
Drug name (generic or brand), strength in metric units, quantity to dispense
Directions for use that are specific to the drug and patient, including purpose and duration; avoid 'take as directed'
Refills and warning labels (e.g. may cause drowsiness, avoid alcohol)
Legible, unambiguous and complete; omissions such as 'continue eye drops' cause errors
Always put a zero before a decimal point (0.1) and never add a trailing zero (1 mg, not 1.0 mg)
Write out 'units', 'microgram' and 'daily' rather than abbreviating; safest to avoid abbreviations altogether
Check for contraindications, interacting drugs (including OTC) and physicochemical incompatibilities

cards.front: Why should a prescription state the purpose of the drug and write directions out in full?
cards.back: Simple, written-out directions with the purpose reduce misreading and omission errors. Abbreviations can be misread: QD is do-not-use, and OD means right eye. Write the drug name, purpose and duration on the label, and give specific directions with few doses and drugs per day. Telling the patient to take as directed leads to confusion, noncompliance and error.

cards.front: Essay: Process of rational prescribing from diagnosis to follow-up

points: Provisional diagnosis; define the therapeutic problem and goals; select the drug class for each goal; choose the drug on efficacy, safety, suitability and cost; decide dose, route and duration; give information; monitor and revise
Expected effect and timing; cure versus control; effect of missed doses; common side effects without alarming; precautions and tests; check that the patient understood
Prescriber and patient details, date, drug name and metric strength, quantity, specific directions, refills and warnings
Avoid leading-zero, trailing-zero, U and microgram errors and ambiguous abbreviations
Reasons for noncompliance and strategies to improve it; review until goals are met; reconcile medicines at care transitions
Matches the criteria of an appropriate prescription and counters the causes of irrational prescribing

cards.front: How does the WHO define essential medicines?
cards.back: Medicines that satisfy the priority health care needs of a population. They are chosen for public health relevance, evidence of efficacy and safety, and comparative cost-effectiveness. They should be available at all times in working health systems, in adequate amounts and suitable dosage forms, with assured quality, adequate information and a price the individual and community can afford.

cards.front: What is an orphan drug, and why do governments support it?
cards.back: A drug or biological for a rare disease, or for a commoner disease endemic only in resource-poor areas, where the cost of developing and marketing it is not expected to be recovered from sales. Under the US Orphan Drug Amendment Act (1983), a rare disease affects fewer than 0.2 million people in the USA. Governments give tax benefits and other incentives to encourage development.

cards.front: What are over-the-counter (OTC) drugs, and how is prescription status regulated in India?
cards.back: OTC drugs can be bought without a prescription because they are relatively harmless, e.g. paracetamol, aspirin, antacids, senna, lactulose, vitamins and ferrous salts. Most drugs, including all antibiotics, are prescription-only; in India they are placed in Schedule H of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules.

cards.front: Short note: Essential drugs (WHO concept)

points: Those that satisfy the priority healthcare needs of the population
Public health relevance
Evidence of efficacy and safety
Comparative cost-effectiveness
Available in functioning health systems at all times, in adequate amounts and suitable dosage forms, with assured quality, information and affordable price

cards.front: Why do countries keep an essential medicines list, and what is it based on?
cards.back: A small set of well-tested, cheaper drugs often meets most health needs as well as newer costly ones, so listing them improves availability, saves cost and promotes rational use. Selection rests on public health relevance, evidence of efficacy and safety, comparative cost-effectiveness and assured quality.

cards.front: Short note: WHO and National List of Essential Medicines

points: First Model List of Essential Drugs in 1977; revised periodically
KDT 8e quotes the 20th list (2017): 433 medicines, including 25 FDCs
Member countries adapt it to local needs
First National Essential Drugs List 1996; revised 2011, then 2015 as the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM)
NLEM 2015 (as given in KDT 8e): 376 medicines, of which 20 are FDCs
Medicines are marked for primary, secondary and tertiary care levels
Basis for procurement and supply, especially in the public sector
Improves availability, saves cost and promotes rational use

cards.front: Short note: 'P' drug (personal drug) concept

points: P-drugs are the few drugs a prescriber chooses for regular use and knows well
Padmaja: about 40 to 60 drugs needed routinely; Satoskar: 50 to 60
Criteria: efficacy, safety, suitability for the patient, and cost
Patient factors such as renal or hepatic disease, diabetes, pregnancy, lactation or allergy can rule a drug out
P-treatment is the first-choice treatment for a given illness
P-treatment is not always a drug, e.g. lifestyle change in obesity
Keep a personal list with dosage form, dose, frequency and duration
Add patient-teaching and monitoring notes; revise the list as new drugs appear
Supports rational prescribing and continued medical education

cards.front: When can a fixed-ratio combination be on the essential list, and how does this differ from its general use?
cards.back: Only when every ingredient is needed, its dose suits the population, and the combination offers a clear advantage over the single drugs. KDT notes that only a handful of FDCs are rational: the WHO 2017 list carries 25 FDCs and India's NLEM 2015 only 20.

cards.front: Essay: Selection criteria for essential medicines

points: Only a small set of medicines meets most health needs
Cheaper, well-tested drugs are often as good as newer, costlier ones
Concentrating resources on this set gives better value
Adequate efficacy and safety data from clinical studies
Quality, including bioavailability, and stability on storage must be assured
Pattern of prevalent diseases
Facilities and trained personnel; financial resources
Genetic, demographic and environmental factors
Compare efficacy, safety, quality, price and availability
Cost-benefit ratio is a major consideration
Pharmacokinetic properties and local manufacturing capacity also count
Mostly single compounds; fixed-ratio combinations only with proven advantage
List is reviewed continuously as disease patterns, evidence and drugs change
Selection should follow rationally developed treatment guidelines

cards.front: When is a fixed-dose combination (FDC) rational? Give the main advantages.
cards.back: When every component is needed at the stated doses. Advantages: better adherence and convenience; synergy (sulfamethoxazole plus trimethoprim, levodopa plus carbidopa); components with different mechanisms add their effect while side effects differ (amlodipine plus atenolol); one component offsets another's side effect (thiazide plus a potassium-sparing diuretic); a single drug cannot be given alone in TB, HIV or falciparum malaria; sometimes cheaper than separate tablets.

cards.front: Complete: disadvantages of fixed-dose combinations
cards.text: The patient may receive {{unneeded}} components; one ingredient's dose cannot be changed without altering the other; components may have different {{time courses}} and renal or hepatic handling; an adverse effect is hard to {{attribute}} to one drug; a {{contraindication}} to one part bars the whole product; and a false sense of {{superiority}} may follow.

cards.front: Classify: examples of rational fixed-dose combinations
cards.text: Sulfamethoxazole + {{trimethoprim}} (synergy); levodopa + {{carbidopa}} (synergy); {{isoniazid}} + rifampin (single-drug use avoided in TB); amlodipine + {{atenolol}} (different mechanisms, antihypertensive); thiazide + {{potassium-sparing diuretic}} (side effect offset).

cards.front: Which drug class must not be given as a fixed-dose combination with other drugs for internal use?
cards.back: Corticosteroids. The reference states they should never be combined with any other drug meant for internal use, because the steroid dose can then not be adjusted on its own.

cards.front: Short note: Irrational fixed-dose combinations

points: Contains an ingredient the patient does not need
Fixed ratio prevents individual dose adjustment
Components with different pharmacokinetics given at one interval
No proven advantage over the single agents
Antimicrobial combinations used without need, adding toxicity and resistance risk
Tonic or vitamin add-ons with no clear benefit
Products containing doubtful-efficacy ingredients
Use a combination only if every component is needed at that dose
Prescribe separate drugs when individual dosing matters
Know the exact composition of any FDC used
Corticosteroids must never be combined with other drugs for internal use (inhalers excepted in the banned list)
Banned examples: penicillin with sulfonamide, tetracycline with vitamin C, vitamins with analgesics or tranquillisers, antihistamines with antidiarrhoeals, more than one antihistamine in one product
KDT 8e: besides the earlier bans, 344 more irrational FDCs were banned in India
The 2017 WHO list has only 25 FDCs and NLEM 2015 only 20

cards.front: A patient on a fixed-dose combination develops an adverse reaction and later renal impairment. What problems arise with the FDC?
cards.back: The offending drug cannot be identified easily, and an allergy or contraindication to one component bars the whole product. In renal or hepatic impairment the components' pharmacokinetics change unequally, yet the dose of one cannot be changed without altering the other. Components with different time courses are also given at one interval, which may suit neither.

cards.front: Why are levodopa plus carbidopa and amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid sold in more than one ratio?
cards.back: Dose individualisation is the main weakness of an FDC, so a few useful combinations are offered at different ratios, e.g. levodopa 100 mg with carbidopa 10 or 25 mg, and amoxicillin 250 or 500 mg with clavulanic acid. Most FDCs have a single ratio and cannot be adjusted.

cards.front: Essay: Fixed-dose combinations - merits, demerits and rational use

points: Two or more drugs in a fixed dose ratio in one preparation

Convenience and adherence; synergy (cotrimoxazole, levodopa-carbidopa); additive effects with different side effects; one drug offsets another's side effect; single drug unsafe in TB, HIV, falciparum malaria; sometimes cheaper

Unneeded drug adds toxicity and cost; dose cannot be individualised; different time courses; altered renal or hepatic function affects components differently; adverse effect cannot be attributed; one contraindication bars the product; false sense of superiority, especially antimicrobials

Prescribe only if every component is needed; corticosteroids never combined for internal use; some combinations banned in India (344 more recently); only a handful are rational (WHO 2017 list: 25, NLEM 2015: 20)
Know the exact composition and use an FDC only when its advantage is proven

cards.front: Complete: pharmacoeconomics
cards.text: Pharmacoeconomics is the branch of {{health economics}} that expresses the {{cost and benefit}} of therapeutic drugs in economic terms; regulators increasingly ask for an {{economic analysis}} alongside evidence of benefit.

cards.front: What is a QALY and how is it used?
cards.back: Quality-adjusted life years combine survival time with health-related quality of life into a single overall measure of therapeutic benefit, and are listed among clinical outcome measures in trials.

cards.front: For which kinds of drugs is plasma level monitoring useful, and for which is it pointless?
cards.back: Useful where the safety margin is low or individual variation is large: digoxin, anticonvulsants, antiarrhythmics, theophylline, aminoglycosides, lithium, and in renal failure, poisoning, unexplained failure or doubtful compliance. Pointless where the response is easily measured (antihypertensives, oral anticoagulants), for prodrugs such as levodopa, hit-and-run drugs and irreversible-action drugs, since plasma level does not track effect.

cards.front: Why can a surrogate end-point mislead, and what do NNT and meta-analysis add to judging a drug?
cards.back: In the CAST trial antiarrhythmics suppressed arrhythmias yet increased mortality compared with placebo, so the surrogate hid harm. NNT is the number of patients to be treated for one to show the effect, benefit or harm. Meta-analysis statistically pools several independent trials.

cards.front: What is evidence-based medicine?
cards.back: The process of systematically finding, critically evaluating and using current research findings as the basis of clinical decisions, instead of the impression of the individual physician.

cards.front: What does a therapeutic evaluation of a drug cover?
cards.back: Quantitation of the benefit it gives; the best way to use it (dose, duration and patient selection); how it compares with other available drugs; and surveillance of the adverse effects it produces.

cards.front: Short note: Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)

points: Narrow safety margin: digoxin, anticonvulsants, antiarrhythmics, theophylline, aminoglycosides, lithium, tricyclic antidepressants
Large individual variation: antidepressants, lithium
Toxic drugs in renal failure: aminoglycosides, vancomycin
Poisoning, to confirm it and track clearance
Unexplained treatment failure (antimicrobials); checking compliance (psychotropics)
Response is easily measured: antihypertensives, hypoglycaemics, diuretics, oral anticoagulants, inhalational anaesthetics
Drug is a prodrug needing activation (levodopa)
Effect outlasts plasma level ('hit and run'): reserpine, MAO inhibitors, omeprazole
Action is irreversible: organophosphates, phenoxybenzamine
Dose adjustment of long-acting drugs: trough level just before the next dose
Short-acting intermittent drugs (ampicillin, gentamicin): sample about 1-2 hours after dosing
Poisoning: sample early and repeat to judge clearance

cards.front: Short note: Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)

points: Low safety margin: digoxin, anticonvulsants, antiarrhythmics, theophylline, aminoglycosides, lithium, TCAs
Large individual variation (e.g. antidepressants, lithium)
Toxic drug in renal failure (e.g. aminoglycosides, vancomycin)
Poisoning; failure of response without obvious cause; checking compliance
Sample timing depends on purpose: dose adjustment vs other purposes
Interval after dosing is critical and drug-specific

cards.front: When should the blood sample be taken for TDM of a long-acting versus a short-acting drug, and why?
cards.back: For dose adjustment of long-acting drugs, sample the steady-state trough just before the next dose; it depends on volume of distribution and clearance. For short-acting drugs such as ampicillin or gentamicin, take a peak sample 1 to 2 h after an oral or i.m. dose. In suspected poisoning take the earliest sample, then repeat to judge clearance and the need for haemodialysis.

cards.front: Why must a clinical trial have a proper control group, and what does a cross-over design gain?
cards.back: The control receives a placebo (where ethical) or the existing standard treatment, and should be as similar to the test group as possible, so that differences can be credited to the drug. In a cross-over design the same patients take both treatments in turn, so they act as their own controls; individual variation is avoided and the sample size may be smaller.

cards.front: Essay: Assessing a drug - therapeutic monitoring and economic evaluation

points: TDM for low-safety-margin drugs, wide variation, renal failure, poisoning, failure and compliance checks
Sampling time: trough for long-acting, peak for short-acting; not useful for prodrugs, hit-and-run or easily measured-response drugs
Physiological, subjective, long-term and quality-of-life measures, QALYs
Surrogate end-points can mislead (CAST); NNT; meta-analysis; ethics committee approval for human experiments
Branch of health economics expressing cost and benefit of drugs; QALY combines survival with quality of life
Regulators ask for economic analysis alongside benefit; controversy over putting money value on health

cards.front: What is antimicrobial stewardship?
cards.back: Rang & Dale use the term 'antibiotic stewardship' for sensible clinical use of existing antibacterials, based on understanding how resistance arises and spreads under the selection pressure of heavy drug use. In practice (GG14): prefer narrower-spectrum drugs when other factors are equal; de-escalate (streamline) from broad empirical cover once the pathogen and sensitivity are known; use monotherapy for definitive treatment unless combination has a proven role; and weigh prophylaxis against resistance, microbiome damage, toxicity and cost.

cards.front: Why is a narrow-spectrum antibiotic preferred for definitive therapy, and where do broad-spectrum drugs fit?
cards.back: Once the organism is known, a narrow-spectrum drug is more effective against it and disturbs the normal flora less. Broad-spectrum drugs belong to empirical therapy, to cover all likely pathogens until bacteriology is available; then therapy is de-escalated.

cards.front: How do antibiotic prophylaxis, treatment and suppressive therapy differ?
cards.back: Primary prophylaxis is given before any infection to cover the likely organisms, e.g. benzathine penicillin against recurrent rheumatic fever or isoniazid alone for TB contacts; it must be weighed against resistance, toxicity and cost. Pre-emptive therapy is early, targeted treatment in high-risk patients when a test shows infection before symptoms, for a short defined course. Treatment targets the infecting organism. Suppressive therapy continues a lower dose, different route or different antibiotic after infection is controlled but not eradicated.

cards.front: When is combining antimicrobials justified?
cards.back: For mixed infections needing several agents (e.g. peritonitis, brain abscess, diabetic foot), for empirical cover in severe infection until bacteriology is known (then stop), to prevent resistance in chronic infections (TB, leprosy, HIV, H. pylori, malaria), and for topical use. Severity alone is not a reason when the organism is known.

cards.front: What principles guide empirical antimicrobial therapy before culture results are known?
cards.back: Make at least a tentative clinical diagnosis; guess the likely organism from the clinical features and local experience; start a specific drug. Use broad cover only when the infection is severe or diagnostic services are unavailable. Review the response and narrow or change treatment on bacteriological findings, avoiding hasty, arbitrary switches.

cards.front: Why are antimicrobial combinations discouraged outside specific indications?
cards.back: They encourage a casual approach to diagnosis; they increase adverse effects (e.g. vancomycin with an aminoglycoside causes excess nephrotoxicity); they raise the risk of superinfection; underdosed non-synergistic drugs can select resistance; and they cost more. Combinations are justified for mixed infections, for empirical cover in severe infection until cultures are known, and for topical use.

cards.front: How should aminoglycoside dosing differ from most antibiotics, and when is a bactericidal drug preferred?
cards.back: Aminoglycosides are concentration-dependent killers with a post-antibiotic effect, so one larger daily dose (e.g. gentamicin) is at least as effective as divided doses and may be less toxic. Bactericidal drugs suit impaired host defence, life-threatening infection and less accessible sites such as SABE.

cards.front: Essay: Antimicrobial stewardship as rational use

points: Rational antimicrobial use means the right drug, dose, route and duration
Goal: best outcome with least harm, resistance and cost
Make at least a tentative clinical diagnosis; collect specimens before starting treatment in serious infection
Guess the likely organism from clinical features and local experience
No antibiotics for viral fevers or non-specific diarrhoea
Prefer a specific, narrower-spectrum drug when other factors are equal
Give full doses; adjust for renal impairment where needed
Never a single drug where multidrug therapy is standard (TB, leprosy, HIV)
Combinations only for synergy, preventing resistance, mixed infections, or temporary empirical cover in severe infection
Prophylaxis only for established indications; avoid prolonged post-operative courses
Review when culture results return; de-escalate to the definitive regimen
Avoid hasty, arbitrary switching of drugs
Irrational use promotes resistance, superinfection, toxicity and cost

cards.front: What is off-label use of a drug?
cards.back: Use of a drug for an indication, route or dose other than the approved one, e.g. another disease or a different dose.

cards.front: Why does off-label prescribing carry risk for the prescriber and the payer?
cards.back: In the US a physician may prescribe for any reasonable purpose, but insurers often refuse to pay unless a recognised compendium supports the use. The prescriber may also face litigation if harm follows.

cards.front: Short note: Off-label use of drugs, with examples

points: Use for a different disease, route or dose than the approved label
Clonidine in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
Diazepam injection given rectally in febrile convulsions and status epilepticus
Azathioprine applied topically in psoriasis and atopic dermatitis
Erythromycin for gastroparesis; SSRIs for fibromyalgia
Cyproheptadine as appetite stimulant; inappropriate in underweight children (CNS depression)
Phentolamine for autonomic hyperreflexia after spinal cord transection
Off-label use is listed among factors affecting safe drug use
Reimbursement and litigation risk for the prescriber

cards.front: Essay: Off-label use of drugs, with examples

points: Indication, route or dose outside the approved use
Legal in some settings, but outside the licensed label
Clonidine in ADHD; rectal diazepam in convulsions; topical azathioprine in psoriasis
Erythromycin in gastroparesis; SSRIs in fibromyalgia
Cyproheptadine for appetite, with caution in underweight children
Phentolamine in autonomic hyperreflexia
Evidence for the new use may be weaker than for the approved use
Reimbursement may be refused without compendium support
Legal exposure if untoward effects follow
Weigh benefit against risk for the individual patient
Know the approved use and the reason for stepping outside it

cards.front: What is direct-to-physician (DTP) marketing?
cards.back: Promotion aimed straight at doctors, using literature based on clinical research; a major source of drug information for them.

cards.front: What belief drives many patients to demand a medicine?
cards.back: Misconception and unrealistic expectation that every complaint needs a drug.

cards.front: Short note: Factors influencing prescribing habits of physicians

points: Knowledge alone does not change prescribing
Role models: following teachers or popular doctors
Heavy patient load leads to routine symptom-based prescribing
Imprecise diagnosis: drugs given to cover all possible causes
Drug promotion and unrealistic claims
Unethical inducements: gifts, dinner parties, conference delegation
Promotional literature can be biased or misleading; creates artificial demand
Demands for medicine; misconceptions
'Pill for every ill' expectation

cards.front: Essay: Factors affecting the prescribing habits of physicians

points: Rational prescribing needs the whole therapeutic set-up, not just the right drug
Knowledge of the prescriber is the main determinant, yet knowledge alone fails
Role models, patient load, attitude to prompt relief, imprecise diagnosis
Promotion and unrealistic claims; unethical inducements
Direct-to-physician marketing; promotional literature may mislead
Demand for medicine; 'pill for every ill' belief
Delayed relief, adverse effects, resistance, financial loss
Check promotional claims against leading medical journals
Follow the stepwise rational prescribing process with monitoring and feedback

cards.front: What extra rules apply to Schedule X drugs in India?
cards.back: Stored under lock and key; prescription kept in duplicate for at least 2 years; no substitute may be given; purchaser's signature on the cash bill.

cards.front: What is a prescription-to-OTC switch?
cards.back: Reclassifying a prescription medicine as over-the-counter because consumers can use it safely without medical supervision.

cards.front: Why were lovastatin and pravastatin refused OTC status?
cards.back: Hyperlipidaemia is chronic and asymptomatic, with serious long-term risk, so diagnosis and ongoing management by a health professional are needed.

cards.front: Short note: OTC drugs and the prescription-to-OTC switch

points: OTC drugs are bought without prescription; generally relatively harmless
Simple analgesics, antacids, laxatives, vitamins and ferrous salts are examples
Prescription drugs are placed in Schedule H of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules (1945)
Other schedules (e.g. X, G) carry their own sale and labelling rules
Costly and rigorous; only drugs a consumer can self-diagnose and safely treat qualify
Oral acyclovir for recurrent genital herpes refused: misdiagnosis and resistance concerns
Naloxone nasal spray and norgestrel switched in 2023 (US)
OTC agents may worsen conditions or interact with prescription drugs
Misuse can cause harm, e.g. high-dose dextromethorphan; phenylpropanolamine withdrawn for haemorrhagic stroke

cards.front: Essay: Over-the-counter drugs, regulation in India and the switch process

points: Drugs usable without medical supervision; relatively harmless classes
Contrast with prescription-only drugs (Schedule H)
Drugs and Cosmetics Rules (1945): Schedule H for prescription drugs
Schedule X: lock-and-key storage, duplicate prescription kept 2 years, no substitution
Schedule G: caution warning on label
Only self-diagnosable, safely self-treated conditions qualify
Lovastatin and pravastatin refused; naloxone and norgestrel switched (2023)
Future candidates include sumatriptan, nicotine replacement and varenicline
OTC products can interact with prescribed drugs or worsen disease
Clinicians should help patients select safe OTC products
Abuse of OTC products (e.g. dextromethorphan) can cause harm

cards.front: What is a counterfeit medicine?
cards.back: A product deliberately and fraudulently mislabelled for identity or source; it may have wrong, missing or insufficient active ingredient, or fake packaging.

cards.front: How does Indian law define a spurious drug?
cards.back: Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act (s.17B): made under another drug's name, substituting or resembling another drug to deceive, bearing a fictitious manufacturer, or wholly or partly substituted.

cards.front: Why do counterfeit medicines harm patients?
cards.back: Unexpected reactions, toxicity, anaphylaxis or treatment failure; fake antibiotics or vaccines give no protection; they can enter legitimate supply and compromise national care.

cards.front: Short note: Counterfeit medicines, examples and solutions

points: Genuine-looking products smuggled in, e.g. Viagra and Cialis
Correct ingredients in wrong amounts: glibenclamide with several times the normal dose, deaths reported
Genuine packaging with undeclared harmful ingredients (orlistat)
Counterfeit packaging with no active ingredient
Mass serialisation: machine-readable serial code on each pack
Forensic markers, cloud supply-chain data, blockchain
Drugs and Cosmetics Act s.17B, strengthened in 2008
Stricter laws, supply-chain vigilance (especially online), periodic sampling and testing
2018 DTAB advice: unique code with SMS check for top 300 brands (voluntary)
WHO IMPACT (2006): international collaboration; SMS verification platforms in Ghana and Nigeria

cards.front: Essay: Counterfeit medications, their issues and solutions

points: Deliberate fraudulent mislabelling of identity or source (WHO)
Spurious drug under Indian law (s.17B)

IMPACT and SMS verification platforms; India's DTAB code proposal

cards.front: What problem does a crowded drug market create for prescribers?
cards.back: A market with many drugs, many of them me-too products of little added value. Large drug supply with ineffective regulation makes choice hard for prescribers, and irrational use follows.

cards.front: Short note: Crowded drug market

points: Market flooded with many drugs and products, so prescribers cannot easily choose
Drives irrational prescribing rather than rational use
Large number of drugs on the market
Ineffective drug regulation
Me-too drugs: copies of existing drugs, pursued for profit with little added innovation
Multiple prescribing: two or more drugs for the same effect
Over-prescribing, with more adverse drug reactions and treatment failure
Costlier me-too drugs raise health-care costs without added benefit
Prescribe by generic name; unbranded quality medicines (Jan Aushadhi)
Rational prescribing and drug regulation

cards.front: What is a me-too drug?
cards.back: A drug that copies an existing drug's action or structure. It may add little benefit, and some cost more than the older drug it replaces.
